stem: See fig 2.11. In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 90^\circ\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), AC = 14, then find AB and BC.
solution:
In \(\triangle ABC\),
\(\angle B = 90^\circ\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(\therefore\) \(\angle C = 60^\circ\)

By \(30^\circ - 60^\circ - 90^\circ\) theorem,

\(BC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times AC\)

\(BC = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14\)

\(BC = 7\)

\(AB = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times AC\)

\(AB = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 14\)

\(AB = 7\sqrt{3}\)

stem: See fig 2.12, In \(\triangle ABC\), seg AD \(\perp\) seg BC, \(\angle C = 45^\circ\), BD = 5 and AC = \(8\sqrt{2}\) then find AD and BC.
solution:
In \(\triangle ADC\)

\(\angle ADC = 90^\circ\), \(\angle C = 45^\circ\), \(\therefore\) \(\angle DAC = 45^\circ\)

\(AD = DC = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \times 8\sqrt{2}\) ... by \(45^\circ - 45^\circ - 90^\circ\) theorem

\(DC = 8\)   \(\therefore\) \(AD = 8\)

\(BC = BD + DC\)

\(\ \ \ \ = 5 + 8\)

\(BC = 13\)

stem: In fig 2.13, \(\angle PQR = 90^\circ\), seg QN \(\perp\) seg PR, PN = 9, NR = 16. Find QN.
solution:
In \(\triangle PQR\), seg QN \(\perp\) seg PR

\(NQ^2 = PN \times NR\) ... theorem of geometric mean

\(\therefore NQ = \sqrt{PN \times NR}\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ = \sqrt{9 \times 16}\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 3 \times 4\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 12\)

See figure 2.14. In \(\triangle PQR\), \(\angle PQR = 90^\circ\), seg QS \(\perp\) seg PR then find \(x\), \(y\), \(z\).

(From fig. 2.14: S lies on seg PR, PS = 10, SR = 8, QS = \(x\), QR = \(y\), PQ = \(z\).)
solution:
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(\angle PQR = 90^\circ\), seg QS \(\perp\) seg PR

\(QS = \sqrt{PS \times SR}\) .......... (theorem of geometric mean)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ = \sqrt{10 \times 8}\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ = \sqrt{5 \times 2 \times 8}\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ = \sqrt{5 \times 16}\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ = 4\sqrt{5}\)

\(\therefore x = 4\sqrt{5}\)

In \(\triangle QSR\), by Pythagoras theorem

\(QR^2 = QS^2 + SR^2\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = \left(4\sqrt{5}\right)^2 + 8^2\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 16 \times 5 + 64\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 80 + 64\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 144\)

\(\therefore QR = 12\)

In \(\triangle PSQ\), by Pythagoras theorem

\(PQ^2 = QS^2 + PS^2\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = \left(4\sqrt{5}\right)^2 + 10^2\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 16 \times 5 + 100\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 80 + 100\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 180\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 36 \times 5\)

\(\therefore PQ = 6\sqrt{5}\)

Hence \(x = 4\sqrt{5}\), \(y = 12\), \(z = 6\sqrt{5}\)

stem: In the right angled triangle, sides making right angle are 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
solution:
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(\angle Q = 90^\circ\)

\(PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2\) (Pythagoras theorem)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 9^2 + 12^2\)

\(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 81 + 144\)

\(PR^2 = 225\)

\(PR = 15\)

Hypotenuse = 15 cm

stem: In \(\triangle LMN\), \(l = 5\), \(m = 13\), \(n = 12\). State whether \(\triangle LMN\) is a right angled triangle or not.
solution:
\(l = 5\), \(m = 13\), \(n = 12\)

\(l^2 = 25\), \(m^2 = 169\), \(n^2 = 144\)

\(\therefore m^2 = l^2 + n^2\)

\(\therefore\) by converse of Pythagoras theorem \(\triangle LMN\) is a right angled triangle.

stem: See fig 2.16. In \(\triangle ABC\), seg AD \(\perp\) seg BC. Prove that: \(AB^2 + CD^2 = BD^2 + AC^2\)
solution:
According to Pythagoras theorem, in \(\triangle ADC\)

\(AC^2 = AD^2 + CD^2\)

\(\therefore AD^2 = AC^2 - CD^2\) ... (I)

In \(\triangle ADB\)

\(AB^2 = AD^2 + BD^2\)

\(\therefore AD^2 = AB^2 - BD^2\) ... (II)

\(\therefore AB^2 - BD^2 = AC^2 - CD^2\) .......... from I and II

\(\therefore AB^2 + CD^2 = AC^2 + BD^2\)

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle C\) is an acute angle, seg AD \(\perp\) seg BC. Prove that:
\(AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 - 2BC \times DC\)
solution:
In the given figure let AB = \(c\), AC = \(b\), AD = \(p\), BC = \(a\), DC = \(x\),
\(\therefore\) BD = \(a - x\)
In \(\triangle ADB\), by Pythagoras theorem
\(c^2 = (a-x)^2 + p^2\)
\(c^2 = a^2 - 2ax + x^2 + p^2\) .......... (I)
In \(\triangle ADC\), by Pythagoras theorem
\(b^2 = p^2 + x^2\)
\(p^2 = b^2 - x^2\) .......... (II)
Substituting value of \(p^2\) from (II) in (I),
\(c^2 = a^2 - 2ax + x^2 + b^2 - x^2\)
\(\therefore c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ax\)
\(\therefore AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 - 2BC \times DC\)
[Note: the textbook prints the four quantities \(p^2\), \(p^2\), \(x^2\) and \(x^2\) as empty boxes for the reader to fill in; they are filled in above.]

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle ACB\) is obtuse angle, seg AD \(\perp\) seg BC. Prove that:
\(AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 + 2BC \times CD\)
solution:
In the figure seg AD \(\perp\) seg BC
Let AD = \(p\), AC = \(b\), AB = \(c\), BC = \(a\) and DC = \(x\).
DB = \(a + x\)
In \(\triangle ADB\), by Pythagoras theorem,
\(c^2 = (a + x)^2 + p^2\)
\(c^2 = a^2 + 2ax + x^2 + p^2\) .......... (I)
Similarly, in \(\triangle ADC\)
\(b^2 = x^2 + p^2\)
\(\therefore p^2 = b^2 - x^2\) .......... (II)
\(\therefore\) substituting the value of \(p^2\) from (II) in (I)
\(\therefore c^2 = a^2 + 2ax + b^2\)
\(\therefore AB^2 = BC^2 + AC^2 + 2BC \times CD\)

stem: In the figure 2.26, seg PM is a median of \(\triangle PQR\). PM = 9 and \(PQ^2 + PR^2 = 290\), then find QR.
solution:
In \(\triangle PQR\), seg PM is a median.
M is the midpoint of seg QR.
\(QM = MR = \frac{1}{2} QR\)
\(PQ^2 + PR^2 = 2PM^2 + 2QM^2\) (by Apollonius theorem)
\(290 = 2 \times 9^2 + 2QM^2\)
\(290 = 2 \times 81 + 2QM^2\)
\(290 = 162 + 2QM^2\)
\(2QM^2 = 290 - 162\)
\(2QM^2 = 128\)
\(QM^2 = 64\)
\(QM = 8\)
\(\therefore QR = 2 \times QM\)
\(= 2 \times 8\)
\(= 16\)

stem: Prove that, the sum of the squares of the diagonals of a rhombus is equal to the sum of the squares of the sides.
solution:
Given : \(\square PQRS\) is a rhombus. Diagonals PR and SQ intersect each other at point T
To prove : \(PS^2 + SR^2 + QR^2 + PQ^2 = PR^2 + QS^2\)
Proof : Diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other.
\(\therefore\) by Apollonius' theorem,
\(PQ^2 + PS^2 = 2PT^2 + 2QT^2\) .......... (I)
\(QR^2 + SR^2 = 2RT^2 + 2QT^2\) .......... (II)
\(\therefore\) adding (I) and (II),
\(PQ^2 + PS^2 + QR^2 + SR^2 = 2(PT^2 + RT^2) + 4QT^2\)
\(= 2(PT^2 + PT^2) + 4QT^2\) .......... (RT = PT)
\(= 4PT^2 + 4QT^2\)
\(= (2PT)^2 + (2QT)^2\)
\(= PR^2 + QS^2\)
(The above proof can be written using Pythagoras theorem also.)
